title: Stroke Symptoms: 10 Warning Signs You Should Never Ignore

excerpt: A brain stroke is a critical medical emergency. Recognizing the early signs of stroke and stroke warning signs can save lives and prevent permanent disability. Here are 10 vital symptoms you must never overlook.
content:
Understanding Brain Stroke: Why Every Minute Counts

A brain stroke occurs when the blood supply to part of your brain is interrupted or reduced, preventing brain tissue from getting oxygen and nutrients. Within minutes, brain cells begin to die at an alarming rate of nearly 1.9 million neurons every minute. This is why neurologists emphasize that "Time is Brain."

Recognizing the early signs of stroke and understanding critical stroke warning signs allows patients to reach a specialized stroke center within the vital "Golden Hour" (first 3 to 4.5 hours), when clot-busting therapies like IV thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy are most effective.

10 Critical Stroke Warning Signs You Must Never Ignore

While strokes can manifest in various ways depending on which vascular territory of the brain is affected, these 10 symptoms of brain stroke require immediate medical intervention:

1. Sudden Facial Drooping or Asymmetry

One side of the face may suddenly droop, feel numb, or appear uneven. When the person tries to smile, the smile may look lopsided or one corner of the mouth may fail to move.

2. Sudden Weakness or Numbness in One Arm or Leg

Unilateral weakness is one of the classic stroke symptoms. A person may suddenly find themselves unable to lift one arm or leg, or feel severe heaviness and numbness on one side of their body.

3. Difficulty Speaking or Slurred Speech (Dysarthria & Aphasia)

Speech may become slurred, garbled, or difficult to understand. Alternatively, the person may struggle to find the right words or be entirely unable to comprehend spoken language.

4. Sudden Loss of Balance, Dizziness, or Incoordination

Sudden vertigo, stumbling, loss of balance, or unexplained clumsiness often points to a stroke affecting the cerebellum or brainstem.

5. Sudden Vision Changes or Loss of Sight

Vision may suddenly become blurry, doubled (diplopia), or completely dark in one or both eyes. This can happen abruptly without any eye pain.

6. Sudden Severe "Thunderclap" Headache

An abrupt, excruciating headache with no known cause—often described by patients as "the worst headache of my life"—can be a sign of a hemorrhagic stroke or subarachnoid hemorrhage.

7. Sudden Confusion or Cognitive Disorientation

The patient may experience sudden difficulty understanding simple instructions, memory lapses, confusion about time or location, or altered mental alertness.

8. Trouble Swallowing (Dysphagia)

A sudden inability to swallow liquids or solids, coughing while attempting to drink water, or sudden choking sensations can indicate brainstem neurological impairment.

9. Numbness on One Side of the Body

Loss of sensation, tingling ("pins and needles"), or feeling like an entire half of the body is detached or asleep is a major warning flag.

10. Transient Ischemic Attacks (TIAs) – The "Mini-Stroke"

Temporary stroke symptoms that resolve within minutes or hours are known as TIAs. They are a serious warning sign that a major stroke may occur in the coming days or weeks and must be investigated immediately.

The B.E. F.A.S.T. Rule for Quick Stroke Identification

To easily remember and identify stroke warning signs, keep the BE FAST protocol in mind:

  • B - Balance: Sudden loss of balance or coordination.
  • E - Eyes: Sudden vision loss or double vision.
  • F - Face: Face drooping on one side.
  • A - Arms: Arm weakness or drifting downwards when raised.
  • S - Speech: Slurred speech or difficulty understanding.
  • T - Time: Time to call emergency services and rush to a stroke-ready hospital.

Dr. Praveen Gupta, Chairman of the Neurosciences Institute at Marengo Asia Hospital, Gurugram, established the first dedicated stroke center in Gurugram. With round-the-clock neuro-intervention facilities, rapid neuro-imaging, advanced mechanical thrombectomy, and comprehensive neuro-rehabilitation, Dr. Praveen Gupta has successfully treated thousands of acute stroke emergencies.

What Does a Neurology Specialist Do?

A neurologist is a specialized physician trained in the diagnosis, investigation, management, and treatment of disorders affecting the central nervous system (the brain and spinal cord) and the peripheral nervous system (nerves and muscles throughout the body).

Because the nervous system controls virtually every voluntary and involuntary function of the human body, neurological conditions can present with a wide variety of symptoms—from persistent headaches and memory lapses to chronic pain, tremors, and sudden weakness.

When Should You Consult a Neurologist Doctor in Gurgaon?

Knowing when a symptom requires a specialist consultation is crucial for timely and effective care. You should schedule an appointment with the best neurologist in Gurgaon if you experience any of the following:

1. Chronic or Severe Headaches and Migraines

If you suffer from frequent headaches that do not respond to over-the-counter pain relievers, headaches accompanied by nausea, visual disturbances, or headaches that wake you from sleep, a neurology specialist can pinpoint the exact cause and prescribe targeted preventive therapy.

2. Seizures, Fits, or Unexplained Fainting Spells

Any episode of loss of consciousness, involuntary jerking of limbs, staring spells, or confusion requires urgent neurological assessment, EEG testing, and brain MRI scans to evaluate for epilepsy or other neurological triggers.

3. Memory Loss, Confusion, or Cognitive Decline

While mild forgetfulness can be part of normal aging, progressive memory problems, difficulty finding words, disorientation in familiar places, or personality changes can be signs of Alzheimer’s disease, vascular dementia, or other reversible metabolic conditions.

4. Persistent Numbness, Tingling, or Burning Nerve Pain

Neuropathy caused by diabetes, vitamin deficiencies, spinal root compression, or autoimmune conditions often presents with "pins and needles" sensations, burning in the feet, or loss of protective feeling in hands and legs.

5. Movement Problems, Tremors, or Muscle Stiffness

Involuntary shaking of hands or chin at rest, slowing of daily movements (bradykinesia), rigid muscles, or unsteady walking are key indications for evaluation for Parkinson’s disease or dystonia.

6. Chronic Dizziness, Vertigo, or Imbalance

Persistent sensations of spinning, lightheadedness, or feeling unsteady while walking can stem from vestibular nerve issues, cerebellar conditions, or inner ear disorders requiring specialized neuro-vestibular testing.

7. Sleep Disorders and Restless Leg Syndrome

Uncontrolled urges to move legs at night, severe insomnia, narcolepsy, or violent dream enactments (REM sleep behavior disorder) often have neurological roots.

content:
Understanding Migraines: Beyond a Regular Headache

A migraine is a complex neurological disorder characterized by recurrent attacks of moderate-to-severe throbbing headache, typically affecting one side of the head. Migraines are frequently accompanied by heightened sensitivity to light (photophobia), sound (phonophobia), smells, as well as severe nausea and vomiting.

For millions of individuals, untreated migraines cause substantial disruption to work productivity, family life, and mental well-being. Finding an effective migraine treatment in Gurgaon begins with consulting a qualified migraine specialist who can accurately distinguish migraine from other headache subtypes.

Common Migraine Symptoms and Phases

Migraine attacks often progress through four distinct phases:

  1. Prodrome: Subtle changes 24-48 hours prior, such as neck stiffness, food cravings, mood shifts, or frequent yawning.
  2. Aura: Visual disturbances (flashing lights, zigzag lines, blind spots), numbness in face/hands, or temporary speech difficulty occurring in about 25-30% of sufferers before the headache starts.
  3. Attack (Headache Phase): Intense throbbing pain, pulsating sensation, severe nausea, and extreme sensitivity to environmental stimuli lasting anywhere from 4 to 72 hours.
  4. Postdrome ("Migraine Hangover"): Exhaustion, confusion, brain fog, and dizziness lasting up to a day after the pain subsides.

When Should You See a Migraine Doctor in Gurgaon?

You should consult a migraine doctor in Gurgaon if you experience:

  • Headaches occurring 4 or more days per month.
  • Attacks that severely limit your ability to work, study, or carry out normal routines.
  • Over-the-counter painkillers (such as paracetamol, NSAIDs, or combination analgesics) no longer providing relief, or leading to medication overuse headaches (rebound headaches).
  • Headaches accompanied by unusual neurological symptoms like double vision, numbness, or weakness.
  • A sudden change in the frequency, duration, or severity of your typical headache pattern.

Modern Migraine Treatment Options in Gurgaon

Under the clinical leadership of Dr. Praveen Gupta, modern migraine treatment combines acute rescue therapies, preventive medications, and advanced neuromodulation:

1. Acute (Abortive) Therapies

Prescribed to stop a migraine attack as soon as it begins. These include selective 5-HT1 agonists (Triptans), gepants (oral CGRP receptor antagonists), and targeted anti-nausea medications.

2. Preventive Pharmacotherapy

For patients with frequent attacks, daily preventive medications reduce attack frequency and severity. Classes include beta-blockers, antiepileptic medications (e.g., topiramate, valproate), and calcium channel blockers.

3. CGRP Monoclonal Antibodies (Anti-CGRP Injections)

The newest revolution in migraine prevention: targeted monthly or quarterly biological therapies (such as Erenumab, Galcanezumab, and Fremanezumab) that specifically block the calcitonin gene-related peptide pathway responsible for migraine pain transmission.

4. Botox Therapy for Chronic Migraine

FDA-approved OnabotulinumtoxinA injections given around specific nerve endings in the forehead, temples, and neck every 12 weeks for patients suffering from chronic migraine (15 or more headache days per month).

5. Lifestyle, Diet, and Trigger Management

Identifying and avoiding common triggers (dehydration, irregular sleep, stress, aged cheese, processed meats, skipped meals) combined with regular aerobic exercise and stress management strategies.

title: Brain Tumour Surgery: When Is Surgery Needed and What Are the Treatment Options?

content:
What Is a Brain Tumour?

A brain tumour is an abnormal mass or growth of cells inside the skull. Brain tumours can be primary (originating directly within brain tissue, meninges, cranial nerves, or pituitary gland) or secondary/metastatic (cancer that has spread to the brain from other parts of the body such as the lungs, breast, or colon).

Furthermore, brain tumours are classified as benign (non-cancerous) or malignant (cancerous). However, because the skull is a rigid bony structure with fixed volume, even benign tumours can cause significant neurological deficits and increased intracranial pressure if left untreated.

Common Symptoms That Warrant Immediate Evaluation

Symptoms depend heavily on the tumour's size, growth rate, and location in the brain:

  • Persistent, worsening headaches (often most severe in the early morning, accompanied by vomiting).
  • New-onset seizures or convulsions in adults with no prior seizure history.
  • Progressive weakness or numbness on one side of the body.
  • Vision problems, such as loss of peripheral vision, blurred vision, or double vision.
  • Cognitive changes, memory loss, confusion, or personality alterations.
  • Difficulty with balance, walking, or speech.

When Is Brain Tumour Surgery Needed?

Brain tumour surgery is typically the cornerstone and first-line treatment for most accessible brain tumours. Surgery serves several vital purposes:

  • Maximal Safe Resection: Removing as much of the tumour mass as safely possible to relieve pressure on vital brain structures.
  • Accurate Histopathological & Molecular Diagnosis: Obtaining tissue biopsy samples to identify the exact tumour grade, genetic mutations, and molecular markers guiding targeted chemotherapy and radiation.
  • Symptom Relief: Decreasing mass effect, reducing cerebral edema, and controlling intractable seizures or neurological deficits.

Advanced Brain Tumour Treatment & Surgical Options

With modern technological breakthroughs, brain tumour surgery in Gurgaon has become remarkably precise, minimizing surgical risk while maximizing tumour removal:

1. Awake Craniotomy

Used for tumours located near eloquent brain regions responsible for speech, language, or motor control. The patient is awake and interacts with the surgical team during critical phases to ensure zero functional loss.

2. Neuronavigation and Intraoperative MRI/CT

GPS-like 3D computerized guidance systems that allow the brain tumour surgeon in Gurgaon to map brain structures with millimeter precision and navigate safely around critical blood vessels and nerve tracts.

3. Fluorescence-Guided Surgery (5-ALA)

Special oral dyes make high-grade tumour cells glow fluorescent pink under blue light during surgery, enabling surgeons to distinguish tumour boundaries from healthy brain tissue.

4. Endoscopic Skull Base Surgery

Minimally invasive keyhole procedures performed through the nostrils for pituitary tumours, craniopharyngiomas, and skull base lesions without external skin incisions.

5. Multidisciplinary Adjuvant Therapy

Following surgery, comprehensive brain tumour treatment may involve stereotactic radiosurgery (Gamma Knife / CyberKnife), targeted radiation therapy, chemotherapy, and personalized immunotherapies.

content:
Understanding Back and Neck Pain: When to Worry?

Almost 80% of adults experience back or neck pain at some point in their lives. The vast majority of episodes resolve with conservative treatments—including rest, physical therapy, ergonomic adjustments, and anti-inflammatory medications.

However, when structural damage to the vertebrae, intervertebral discs, or spinal ligaments begins compressing the spinal cord or exiting nerve roots, spine surgery may become necessary to protect long-term nerve function and prevent irreversible paralysis.

Red-Flag Signs Indicating Spine Surgery May Be Needed

If you experience any of the following symptoms, you should seek immediate evaluation by a spine and neurology specialist:

1. Progressive Muscle Weakness (e.g., Foot Drop)

Difficulty lifting the front part of your foot (causing it to drag while walking), sudden weakness in your hands leading to dropping objects, or knee buckling indicate severe nerve root compression requiring urgent intervention.

2. Radiating Pain (Sciatica or Cervical Radiculopathy)

Sharp, electric-shock-like pain that shoots down the leg past the knee or travels down the arm into the fingers, especially when accompanied by persistent numbness or reflex loss.

3. Loss of Bowel or Bladder Control (Cauda Equina Syndrome)

Emergency Alert: Sudden difficulty urinating, urinary incontinence, loss of bowel control, or numbness around the groin and inner thighs ("saddle anesthesia") is a medical emergency known as Cauda Equina Syndrome that demands surgical decompression within 24 to 48 hours.

4. Severe Pain Refractory to Conservative Treatment

Incapacitating back or neck pain that fails to improve after 6 to 12 weeks of comprehensive physical therapy, targeted pain management, and medications.

5. Spinal Instability and Deformity

Progressive spinal curvature (scoliosis, kyphosis) or vertebral slippage (spondylolisthesis) causing chronic nerve pinching and severe postural imbalance.

Common Types of Spine & Back Surgery

Modern surgical techniques prioritize tissue preservation, smaller incisions, and rapid recovery:

  • Microdiscectomy: Removal of a herniated disc fragment that is pinching a spinal nerve, performed using a high-powered microscope through a tiny keyhole incision.
  • Laminectomy / Decompression: Removal of the bony lamina to relieve pressure on the spinal canal in patients with lumbar spinal stenosis.
  • Spinal Fusion Surgery: Joining two or more vertebrae permanently using bone grafts and specialized titanium screws/rods to stabilize an unstable spine.
  • Artificial Disc Replacement (Arthroplasty): Replacing a damaged disc with a prosthetic device that preserves normal spinal motion, common in the cervical spine.
  • Minimally Invasive Spine Surgery (MISS): Utilizing tubular retractors and endoscopes to minimize muscle cutting, significantly reducing postoperative pain and hospital stays.

What to Expect During Spine Surgery Recovery

Thanks to minimally invasive techniques, spine surgery recovery is faster and smoother than ever before:

  • Most patients are encouraged to stand and walk within 24 hours of surgery.
  • Hospital stay is typically 1 to 3 days for minimally invasive procedures.
  • Structured physical therapy begins within a few weeks to rebuild core strength and spinal flexibility.
  • Desk workers often return to light duties within 2 to 4 weeks, with full recovery achieved in 2 to 3 months.

Consult Top Brain & Spine Experts in Gurgaon

At Dr. Praveen Gupta's clinic and Marengo Asia Hospital, every patient undergoes a comprehensive neurological assessment before surgery is ever recommended. We champion conservative therapy first, reserving surgery strictly for when it delivers definitive, life-enhancing outcomes.

title: Parkinson's Disease: Early Symptoms and Treatment Options
author: Dr. Praveen Gupta
image_alt: Parkinson's disease early symptoms and advanced treatment options

content:
What Is Parkinson's Disease?

Parkinson's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder of the central nervous system that primarily impacts movement and coordination. It occurs when dopamine-producing nerve cells (neurons) in a vital brain structure called the substantia nigra deteriorate or die.

Dopamine serves as a chemical messenger between the brain and muscles. As dopamine levels drop, patients experience hallmark motor symptoms alongside a wide array of non-motor symptoms.

Early Signs of Parkinson's Disease You Should Know

Recognizing the early signs of Parkinson's disease is critical because neuroprotective and symptomatic treatments are most effective when initiated early:

1. Resting Tremor

A slight shaking or tremor in a finger, hand, or thumb when the limb is relaxed (often called a "pill-rolling" tremor). Tremors usually start on one side of the body before eventually progressing to both.

2. Slowness of Movement (Bradykinesia)

Daily tasks take significantly longer to complete. Patients notice difficulty buttoning shirts, tying shoelaces, getting out of deep chairs, or walking with a shuffling gait.

3. Muscle Stiffness and Rigidity

Unusual stiffness in the limbs or trunk that restricts range of motion and often causes dull, aching muscle pain (often misdiagnosed as arthritis or frozen shoulder).

4. Micrographia (Shrinking Handwriting)

Handwriting noticeably becomes much smaller, cramped, and crowded together as sentences progress across the page.

5. Loss of Facial Expression ("Masked Face")

A reduced blink rate and fixed facial expression, making the person appear serious, depressed, or unblinking even when engaged in lively conversation.

6. Soft or Monotone Voice (Hypophonia)

Speaking in a very quiet, raspy, or breathy tone without normal vocal inflection.

7. Non-Motor Symptoms

  • Loss of sense of smell (Anosmia) occurring years before motor symptoms.
  • Chronic constipation refractory to diet.
  • REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (physically acting out vivid dreams, flailing limbs during sleep).
  • Anxiety, depression, and mood fluctuations.

Comprehensive Parkinson's Treatment Options

While there is currently no cure for Parkinson's disease, modern Parkinson's treatment can dramatically reduce symptoms and allow patients to maintain an independent, high-quality life for decades:

1. Dopaminergic Medications

  • Levodopa / Carbidopa: The gold standard therapy that converts directly into dopamine inside the brain.
  • Dopamine Agonists: Medications that mimic dopamine effects in the brain (e.g., Pramipexole, Ropinirole).
  • MAO-B and COMT Inhibitors: Drugs that prevent the enzymatic breakdown of dopamine in the brain and bloodstream.

2. Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) Surgery

For patients with advanced Parkinson's experiencing motor fluctuations, wearing-off episodes, or medication-induced dyskinesias (involuntary writhing), Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) is a revolutionary surgical treatment. Thin electrodes are implanted into specific brain targets (such as the subthalamic nucleus or globus pallidus) connected to an internal pulse generator in the chest, restoring smooth motor control.

3. Dedicated Rehabilitation & Lifestyle Therapy

Targeted physical therapy (including gait training and balance exercises), speech therapy (LSVT LOUD), occupational therapy, and regular aerobic exercise (cycling, boxing, swimming) have proven neuroprotective benefits.

title: Why Do I Have Frequent Headaches? Common Causes and When to Worry
author: Dr. Praveen Gupta
image_alt: Frequent headaches causes, chronic headache symptoms and when to worry

meta_description: Struggling with frequent headaches or constant headache pain? Learn primary vs secondary headache causes, red-flag symptoms, and specialized neurological treatments.
excerpt: Frequent headaches can disrupt your daily life. Learn the most common headache causes, the difference between primary and secondary chronic headaches, and when to seek medical care.
content:
Why Do Frequent Headaches Happen?

Headaches are among the most common medical complaints worldwide. While occasional headaches are usually benign and linked to stress, lack of sleep, or dehydration, frequent headaches and chronic headaches (occurring 15 or more days a month for at least three months) require thorough neurological evaluation.

To understand why you have a constant headache, neurologists divide headaches into two main categories: Primary Headaches and Secondary Headaches.

Primary Headache Causes

Primary headaches are standalone conditions caused by overactivity of pain-sensitive structures in the head and brain, rather than an underlying disease:

1. Tension-Type Headaches

The most prevalent type of headache. It feels like a tight band squeezing around the forehead, temples, or back of the neck. Often triggered by emotional stress, poor posture, prolonged screen time, and eye strain.

2. Migraines

Throbbing, pulsating pain usually on one side of the head, worsened by physical activity and accompanied by nausea, vomiting, photophobia (light sensitivity), and phonophobia (sound sensitivity).

3. Cluster Headaches

Excruciating, piercing pain around or behind one eye, occurring in cyclical clusters (several times a day for weeks). Often accompanied by eye redness, tearing, and nasal congestion on the affected side.

4. Medication Overuse Headaches (Rebound Headaches)

Paradoxically, frequent use of over-the-counter painkillers (more than 10-15 days a month) can trigger chronic daily rebound headaches as the medication wears off.

Secondary Headache Causes: When Headaches Are a Symptom of Something Else

Secondary headaches stem from an underlying medical or structural problem, such as:

  • Sinusitis: Inflammation of nasal sinuses causing facial pressure and forehead ache.
  • Cervicogenic Headache: Neck arthritis or cervical spine nerve irritation radiating upward to the head.
  • Hypertension: Extremely high blood pressure causing morning throbbing.
  • Temporomandibular Joint (TMJ) Dysfunction: Jaw clenching and teeth grinding.
  • Intracranial Pathology: Brain tumours, aneurysms, meningitis, or intracranial hypertension.

When to Worry: Red Flag Symptoms (S.N.O.O.P. Criteria)

Consult a neurologist immediately if your headache is accompanied by any of these warning signs:

  • S - Systemic Symptoms: Fever, unexplained weight loss, stiff neck, or rash.
  • N - Neurological Deficits: Weakness, numbness, confusion, vision loss, or speech difficulty.
  • O - Onset Sudden (Thunderclap): Peak excruciating intensity reached within seconds.
  • O - Older Age Onset: New headaches starting after age 50.
  • P - Pattern Change: Progressive worsening in frequency or severity compared to past headaches.
  • Headaches that wake you from deep sleep or worsen significantly when bending over or coughing.

How Dr. Praveen Gupta Treats Chronic Headaches

Successful management begins with identifying the root cause through advanced neuro-imaging (MRI/MRA) and specialized headache profiling. Treatment protocols include targeted preventive medications, lifestyle optimization, trigger avoidance, nerve blocks, and Botox therapy for chronic cases.

If frequent headaches are impacting your quality of life, schedule an appointment with Dr. Praveen Gupta in Gurgaon for comprehensive relief.

title: Why Is One Side of My Body Numb? Causes You Should Not Ignore
author: Dr. Praveen Gupta

excerpt: Feeling numbness on one side of body or persistent one sided numbness? Learn the crucial causes—from acute stroke to spinal cord compression and neuropathy—and when to seek emergency help.
content:
Understanding One-Sided Numbness (Hemiparesthesia & Hemihypesthesia)

Waking up or suddenly feeling that one side of your body is numb is an alarming symptom that should never be ignored. Numbness refers to a partial or total loss of sensation, often accompanied by numbness and tingling (paresthesia), burning, or a "pins-and-needles" sensation.

Because the sensory pathways travel from sensory receptors in your skin, up through peripheral nerves, into the spinal cord, and cross over to the sensory cortex in the opposite hemisphere of the brain, one sided numbness indicates a problem along this complex neurological circuit.

Major Causes of Numbness on One Side of the Body

1. Acute Brain Stroke (Medical Emergency)

The most urgent and critical cause of sudden one-sided numbness is a stroke or Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA). When a blood clot blocks blood flow to the thalamus or parietal cortex of the brain, sensation on the opposite side of the face, arm, and leg is abruptly lost.

Warning: If one-sided numbness occurs suddenly, especially alongside face drooping, arm weakness, speech difficulty, or confusion, call emergency services immediately.

2. Spinal Cord Compression & Herniated Discs

A severely herniated disc in the neck (cervical spine) or back (thoracic/lumbar spine) can compress the spinal cord or exiting nerve roots (Brown-Séquard syndrome or severe radiculopathy), causing numbness and weakness radiating down one arm or leg.

3. Multiple Sclerosis (MS)

Multiple Sclerosis is an autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks the myelin sheath protecting nerve fibers in the central nervous system. MS plaques in the brain or spinal cord frequently cause unilateral sensory loss, numbness, and visual disturbances in young adults.

4. Hemiplegic Migraine

A rare, specialized subtype of migraine where the aura includes temporary unilateral numbness, tingling, and weakness that mimics a stroke. It must be carefully evaluated by a neurologist to rule out vascular causes.

5. Peripheral Neuropathy & Nerve Entrapment

Compression of specific peripheral nerves—such as the median nerve in Carpal Tunnel Syndrome, the ulnar nerve at the elbow, or the peroneal nerve at the knee—can cause distinct patches of numbness and tingling, although typically localized to a specific limb rather than the entire half of the body.

6. Brain Tumours or Vascular Malformations

A slow-growing mass, aneurysm, or arteriovenous malformation (AVM) pressing against sensory pathways in the brain can produce gradually progressive one-sided sensory loss over weeks or months.

When to Seek Emergency Medical Attention

Go to the nearest emergency department if one-sided numbness is accompanied by:

  • Sudden onset within seconds or minutes.
  • Weakness, paralysis, or heaviness in the arm or leg.
  • Facial drooping or uneven smile.
  • Slurred speech or difficulty finding words.
  • Sudden loss of vision, balance, or consciousness.
